einzeiler: Songwriter and producer David Porter on building the Stax sound and writing hits.
kurzfassung: David Porter discusses his legendary career as a songwriter and producer for Stax Records alongside Isaac Hayes. He details their collaborative writing process, crafting hits for Sam and Dave, and growing up in Memphis. Porter also shares stories about working with Otis Redding and the true nature of the Stax community.
stichpunkte: Defining the Stax sound as a pursuit of pure emotional connection
Developing signature bass and horn patterns to stand apart from Motown
Using head arrangements to build songs collectively in the studio without reading music
Writing Sam and Dave's Hold On, I'm Coming from a bathroom joke and a Superman inspiration
Growing up on a remarkable Memphis street alongside Maurice White and members of the Bar-Kays
Meeting Estelle Axton and launching the R&B era of Stax Records through an audition
Clarifying that the eventual decline of Stax was not caused by racial division
Explaining how the sloped floor of the former theater created a natural delay for the rhythm section
Running a free nonprofit organization called The Consortium MMT to mentor young musicians

kapitel.titel: Growing Up in Memphis and Early Influences
The Reality of Stax Unity and Studio Acoustics
Giving Back Through The Consortium MMT

clips.hook: We knew that we cannot do Motown better than Motown.
clips.text: Recognizing the immense success of competitors like Motown and Burt Bacharach, the producers realized they needed to establish their own distinctive identity instead of trying to replicate existing styles.

clips.hook: I went to the restroom, and Isaac was trying to rush me out.
clips.text: A classic hit song was born from a rushed bathroom break late at night when a simple verbal exchange sparked a creative breakthrough.

clips.hook: The people they hired were educators.
clips.text: Radio station DJs who also worked as high school teachers served as powerful role models by effortlessly bridging the worlds of media and education.

clips.hook: I literally went to school and talked to Mr. Martin.
clips.text: A high school student was pulled straight out of class by a popular older alumnus to play baritone horn on a pivotal recording session.

clips.hook: There was a natural delay that Al had to adapt to.
clips.text: The physical layout of the converted movie theater forced the drummer to establish a unique groove to compensate for the distance from the amplifiers.

beschreibung:
David Porter's story goes well beyond writing songs and releasing albums for Stax Records. His recent memoir, The Soul Man, tells how he and his partner Isaac Hayes helped invent a sound rich and enduring enough to define American music from the 1960s to today. Together they wrote and produced hits for Sam & Dave, Johnnie Taylor, and dozens of other artists, and in the process built what became known as the Stax sound, a sound Porter still describes as the pursuit of pure emotional connection.
Porter grew up on a dead-end street in Memphis that also produced Maurice White of Earth, Wind & Fire and members of the Bar-Kays. He started out singing in church before eventually singing and producing music for Stax. He never learned to read music. None of the great names at Stax did. Instead, they built songs by ear, in the room, together, a process Porter calls “head arrangements,” and it became the foundation for some of the greatest songs in the history of R&B.
Today, Bruce Headlam sits down with David Porter to talk about how he and Isaac Hayes built a signature sound to set themselves apart from Motown, Burt Bacharach and Hal David. He also recalls the writing session that turned a bathroom joke into Sam & Dave's "Hold On, I'm Coming," and the incredible story of how Otis Redding went from an artist's personal driver to a Stax superstar.
